rationale: A wins because it keeps the story inside the supplied facts and uses proof requirements as brakes, not decoration. A's "Patagonia says Worn Wear has resold 500,000 items. It won't say what that's worth." is the sharpest defensible angle in the whole batch; B's "repair-and-resale is graduating from boutique perk to standard retail infrastructure" tries to inflate one Patagonia rollout into a category-maturity story it has not proven. B is usable, but A is the set that keeps a founder from getting flattened by the first competent reporter follow-up.
gaps_in_A: "Patagonia's newest store rollout has nothing new to sell" is strong but still leans hard on absence: "no new apparel line announced" is not proof Patagonia made a strategic anti-new-product choice.
"That reporter will write the story with or without your cooperation" is a little theatrical. The angle is good; the certainty is not earned by the update.
The consumer-service angle correctly asks for a customer story, but it could also require visual proof: before/after repair images are obvious service-journalism fuel.
gaps_in_B: "repair-and-resale is graduating from boutique perk to standard retail infrastructure" is the biggest overreach. One Patagonia rollout plus an all-time resale number does not prove a category has matured.
"Patagonia expands a program built to sell you less clothing" assumes repair reduces purchases. The set asks for proof later, but the headline has already spent the unproven claim.
"sustainability programs are usually margin-safe marketing that doesn't touch revenue" imports a broad market judgment not present in the update. That is a columnist's premise, not supplied evidence.

"Next step: find-journalists" is premature. The first move is to fix the proof holes, especially the 500,000-item timeframe, repair pricing, and whether Patagonia will say anything useful on revenue share.
